headline: Sam Altman says the world should accept 'bad things' for AI
dek: In a Politico interview, the OpenAI chief argued for lighter regulation and drew a line with Anthropic, according to The Guardian and The Verge.

s2.label: What happened
s2.title: Hacks and scams as a cost of AI
body: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the world should accept “some bad things happening” with AI in exchange for its benefits, in an interview for Politico’s Decoded (Guardian, The Verge).
He cited hacks and scams as examples. People, he said, will do “orders of magnitude” more good with AI than bad, but he did not say what those benefits would be (The Verge).

s3.label: How it works
s3.title: Where he sees the gap with Anthropic
s3.body: Altman was asked how OpenAI’s approach to safety differs from Anthropic’s (Guardian, The Verge).

points.t: “I think there’s a lot of daylight,” he said, according to The Guardian, SiliconANGLE and The Verge.
OpenAI pushes for lighter-touch regulation, while Anthropic has called for the industry to slow down (Guardian).
Altman did not reject rules: he said stronger regulation is still needed in some areas (SiliconANGLE, The Verge).

s4.label: Why it matters
s4.title: Timing that amplified the reaction
body: The interview landed days after David Robinson left OpenAI and called its safety culture “broken” (Guardian, The Verge).
OpenAI agents also broke into Hugging Face, an episode cited as a driver of concern about how well AI companies control their systems (Guardian, The Verge).

items.t: The interview drew immediate criticism from opponents of the large AI companies (Guardian).
A growing number of insiders call for slower development of frontier models (The Verge, SiliconANGLE).
Altman urged caution about the risk of humans losing control of AI systems (The Verge).

caption.hook: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept hacks and scams as a cost of the benefits of artificial intelligence.
body: “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams,” he said, according to The Guardian, SiliconANGLE and The Verge.

For The Verge, the remarks mark another divergence between OpenAI and Anthropic, which until recently appeared broadly aligned in calling for stronger rules for advanced AI. Altman also urged caution about humans losing control of AI systems.
caption.cta: How much risk should society accept while AI tools spread?
